evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Hughes et al., 2018; Torda et al., 2018).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature (Alvarez-Filip et al., 2009).

claim: The relationship between species richness or functional diversity and ecosystem functioning is still poorly understood.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Bulleri et al., 2016; Loreau, 2000).

claim: The dynamics of the benthic community emerge from species traits and the imposed disturbance regime, larval connectivity, sedimentation, and grazing pressure intensity.
source: Emergence: The dynamics of the benthic community emerge from species traits and the imposed disturbance regime (waves, cyclone, thermal stress), larval connectivity, sedimentation, and grazing pressure intensity (which can also emerge from reef rugosity).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's emergent properties.

claim: Cell agents do not make decisions and their behavior results from imposed deterministic or probabilistic rules.
source: Cell agents do not make decisions and their behavior results from imposed deterministic or probabilistic rules.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's agent behavior.

claim: The outcome of a coral-coral interaction is determined by its specific pairwise outcome probabilities.
source: The outcome of a coral-coral interaction is determined by its specific pairwise outcome probabilities
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's interaction rules.

claim: The probability of coral-algae interactions are the same for all coral species.
source: the probability of coral-algae interactions are the same for all coral species
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's interaction rules.

claim: Algae-algae interactions result in a stand-off except when competing against crustose coralline algae.
source: and algae-algae interactions result in a stand-off except when competing against crustose coralline algae.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's interaction rules.

claim: Branching and plating species have the capacity to overtop other colonies and algae depending on their size.
source: Branching and plating species also have the capacity to overtop other colonies and algae depending on their size (Appendix 2: §7.5).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's interaction rules.

claim: The model draws success or failure outcomes each time a patch of algae is grazed, a larva attempts to settle and survive the first 6 months, an agent tries to convert another living agent, and a colony is thermally stressed.
source: Stochasticity: The model draws success or failure outcomes each time a patch of algae is grazed, a larva attempts to settle and survive the first 6 months, an agent tries to convert another living agent (Appendix 2: §7.1, 7.2, 7.5), and a colony is thermally stressed (i.e. bleaching and bleaching-induced mortality; Appendix 2: §7.4).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's stochastic elements.

claim: During initialization, colonies are created and placed randomly in space.
source: During initialization, colonies are created and placed randomly in space
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: Colony sizes are drawn from right-skewed frequency distributions during initialization.
source: their sizes are drawn from right-skewed frequency distributions (Appendix 2: §5.1).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: Grazing and larval settlement happen randomly in space in the model.
source: Finally, grazing and larval settlement happen randomly in space.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's spatial processes.

claim: Four types of data are collected during a simulation: percentage cover of each taxon, number of recruits for each coral species m⁻², planar area of each colony species⁻¹, and optionally, the rugosity created by the coral colonies.
source: Observation: Four types of data are collected during a simulation: (i) percentage cover of each taxon, (ii) number of recruits for each coral species m−2, (iii) planar area of each colony species−1, and (iv) optionally, the rugosity created by the coral colonies (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's outputs.

claim: The initial composition of the benthic community is defined by the user and is imported from a comma-delimited text file.
source: The initial composition of the benthic community (i.e. the cover of coral species, algae, barren ground, and sand) is defined by the user and is imported from a comma-delimited text file.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: The space is filled first by creating circular coral colonies randomly in space during initialization.
source: The space is filled first by creating circular coral colonies randomly in space.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: Circular patches of algae (314 cm²) are created after coral colonies during initialization.
source: Circular patches of algae (314 cm2) are then created
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: The remaining agents are converted into barren ground and sand during initialization.
source: and the remaining agents are converted into barren ground and sand (Appendix 2: §5).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's initialization.

claim: At each time step, the model imports values for the surface grazed, number of external larvae settling, intensity of waves or cyclones, thermal stress intensity, and sand cover.
source: At each time step, the model imports values for the corresponding period of the (i) surface grazed (%), (ii) number of external larvae settling, (iii) intensity of waves of cyclones (in dislodgement mechanical threshold, a dimensionless measure of the mechanical threshold imposed by waves and cyclones), (vi) thermal stress intensity (in degree-heating weeks), and (v) sand cover (%).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's inputs.

claim: The reef is grazed by randomly selecting circular patches of agents (29 cm²) until a certain percentage cover is reached.
source: The reef is grazed by randomly selecting circular patches of agents (29 cm2) until a certain percentage cover is reached.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's grazing process.

claim: The cover to reach during grazing can be either exclusively imposed or can result from the rugosity that coral colonies create if the rugosity-grazing feedback process is activated.
source: The cover to reach can be either exclusively imposed (imported from a file) or it can result from the rugosity that coral colonies create if the rugosity-grazing feedback process is activated.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's grazing process.

claim: Coral larvae locally produced and arriving from the regional pool attempt to settle in the reef at a random location.
source: Coral larvae locally produced and arriving from the regional pool attempt to settle in the reef at a random location.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's reproduction process.

claim: The number of larvae produced locally for each species depends on species traits and the distribution of colony planar areas in their population.
source: The number of larvae produced locally for each species depends on species traits (i.e. polyp fecundity, corallite area, growth form, sexual system)—we used geometric formulae from McWilliam et al. (2018b) to calculate colony surface area from planar area—and the distribution of colony planar areas in their population
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's reproduction process, with a citation (McWilliam et al. (2018b)).

claim: Species with a brooding mode of larval development release larvae ready to settle and are not affected by water retention time.
source: Species with a brooding mode of larval development release larvae ready to settle and are not affected by water retention time (Appendix 2: §7.2.1.1).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's reproduction process.

claim: Larvae have a chance of settling successfully on barren ground, crustose coralline algae, and dead coral agents.
source: Larvae have a chance of settling successfully on barren ground, crustose coralline algae, and dead coral agents.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's settlement process.

claim: Algae recruit at the end of a time step by filling up the remaining available space.
source: Algae recruit at the end of a time step by filling up the remaining available space (i.e. ungrazed barren ground and dead coral agents) (Appendix 2: §7.2.2).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's algae recruitment process.

claim: The model modelled colony dislodgment using colony shape factor from Madin and Connolly (2006).
source: We modelled colony dislodgment using colony shape factor from Madin and Connolly (2006), which is compared for each colony to the intensity of the disturbance (expressed as dislodgement mechanical threshold).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's dislodgment process, with a citation (Madin and Connolly (2006)).

claim: The model implemented branching-colony fragmentation by modifying the relationship between fragment size and survival established by Highsmith et al. (1980).
source: We implemented branching-colony fragmentation by modifying the relationship between fragment size and survival established by Highsmith et al. (1980).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's fragmentation process, with a citation (Highsmith et al. (1980)).

claim: The authors defined their own models to simulate the effect on the algae community because no relationships have been established empirically.
source: We defined our own models to simulate the effect on the algae community because no relationships have been established empirically (Appendix 2: §7.3).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's algae disturbance process.

claim: The model first defined a species-specific index of bleaching susceptibility using bleaching-resistance traits and the bleaching response index from Swain et al. (2016b).
source: We first defined a species-specific index of bleaching susceptibility using bleaching-resistance traits and the bleaching response index from Swain et al. (2016b).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's bleaching process, with a citation (Swain et al. (2016b)).

claim: The model used the bleaching susceptibility index to establish species-specific logistic bleaching responses as a function of the intensity of the thermal stress using data from Eakin et al. (2010).
source: We then used this index to establish species-specific logistic bleaching responses as a function of the intensity of the thermal stress (in degree heating-week) using data from Eakin et al. (2010).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's bleaching process, with a citation (Eakin et al. (2010)).

claim: Coral and algae agents on the edge of their colony or patch attempt to convert neighbouring agents within a certain radius.
source: Coral and algae agents on the edge of their colony or patch attempt to convert neighbouring agents within a certain radius.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's growth process.

claim: The size of the radius for growth depends on the species growth rate and the state of the neighbouring agents.
source: The size of the radius depends on the species growth rate and the state of the neighbouring agents
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's growth process.

claim: The model simulated the effect of direct competition with a living agent on growth rate by reducing the length of the radius.
source: we simulated the effect of direct competition with a living agent on growth rate by reducing the length of the radius.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's competition process.

claim: The model used competitive outcome probabilities from Precoda et al. (2017) to simulate between coral interactions.
source: We used competitive outcome probabilities from Precoda et al. (2017) to simulate between coral interactions (we used the trait aggressiveness if the species were not present in their list; see Appendix 1) (Appendix 2: §7.5.2).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's competition process, with a citation (Precoda et al. (2017)).

claim: The model used empirical estimates of competitive outcome probability to simulate competition between coral and algae.
source: We used empirical estimates of competitive outcome probability to simulate competition between coral and algae (Brown et al., 2017; K. T. Brown, personal communication, October 2017; Appendix 2: §7.5.3).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's competition process, with citations (Brown et al., 2017; K. T. Brown, personal communication, October 2017).

claim: The model considered algal functional groups as equal competitors and therefore they cannot overgrow each other, except for crustose coralline algae, which is a weaker competitor.
source: We considered algal functional groups as equal competitors and therefore they cannot overgrow each other, except for crustose coralline algae, which is a weaker competitor (Appendix 2: §7.5.4).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the model's algae competition process.

claim: The authors used data collected between November 2001 and July 2011 in three sites located in Martinique in the Caribbean for model calibration.
source: We used data collected between November 2001 and July 2011 in three sites located in Martinique in the Caribbean: Fond Boucher (14° 39′ 21.07″ N, 61° 09′ 38.98″ W), Pointe Borgnesse (14° 26′ 48.74″ N, 60° 54′ 12.72″ W), and Ilet à Rats (14° 40′ 58.04″ N, 60° 54′ 1.18″ W).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the data used for calibration.

claim: The data were collected biannually by the Observatoire du Milieu Marin Martiniquais for the program Initiative Française pour les REcifs COralliens.
source: The data were collected biannually (once per dry and wet seasons) by the Observatoire du Milieu Marin Martiniquais (OMMM) for the program Initiative Française pour les REcifs COralliens (IFRECOR).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the data collection.

claim: The authors downloaded values of degree-heating weeks for the corresponding location from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data server ERDDAP.
source: We downloaded values of degree-heating weeks for the corresponding location from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data server ERDDAP (Environmental Research Division's Data Access Program; coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap) (Appendix 3—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the data sources.

claim: The authors identified cyclone tracks using the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Historical Hurricane Tracks website.
source: We identified cyclone tracks using the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Historical Hurricane Tracks website (coast.noaa.gov/hurricanes).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the data sources.

claim: The authors modelled thermal stress by inputting at each time step the maximum degree-heating week value found for the corresponding period.
source: We modelled thermal stress by inputting at each time step the maximum degree-heating week value found for the corresponding period.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors represented the intensity of hydrodynamic regimes by inputting values of the dislodgement mechanical threshold.
source: We represented the intensity of hydrodynamic regimes by inputting values of the dislodgement mechanical threshold (Madin and Connolly, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology, with a citation (Madin and Connolly, 2006).

claim: Hurricane Dean affected the reefs in August 2007, with its intensity changing from Category 1 to 2 while passing over Martinique.
source: We imposed a constant value in the absence of cyclone and a lower value when Hurricane Dean affected the reefs in August 2007 (its intensity changed from Category 1 to 2 while passing over Martinique).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about a historical event used in the calibration.

claim: The authors defined three different hydrodynamic regimes that were included in the calibration procedure for each site.
source: Because of this uncertainty, we defined three different hydrodynamic regimes that we included in the calibration procedure for each site (Appendix 3—figure 5).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors defined models predicting grazing intensity as a function of herbivorous fish and urchin density using empirical data from Williams and Polunin (2001) and Sammarco (1980).
source: To estimate the percentage of the reef grazed at each time step, we first defined models predicting grazing intensity (i.e. percentage cover maintained in a cropped state) as a function of herbivorous fish and urchin density (we did not activate the rugosity-grazing feedback process). We defined these models using the empirical data from Williams and Polunin (2001) and Sammarco (1980) for fish and urchins, respectively (Appendix 3—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology, with citations (Williams and Polunin (2001) and Sammarco (1980)).

claim: The authors defined three additional similar grazing regimes of different intensities, which were included in the calibration procedure.
source: Finally, we defined three additional similar regimes of different intensities, which we included in the calibration procedure (Appendix 3—figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The model adjusts the amount of sand cover at each time step according to the observed cover measured in each site.
source: The model adjusts the amount of sand cover (i.e. by removing or adding sand patches) at each time step according to the observed cover measured in each site (Appendix 3—figure 4).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors set the number of larvae m⁻² to 700 during each reproductive time period.
source: Having no information about larval connectivity at the three sites, we set the number of larvae m−2to 700 during each reproductive time period (i.e. once a year).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors calibrated the model for each site independently.
source: We calibrated the model for each site independently.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors selected 12 parameters, for which they defined between two to five potential values for calibration.
source: We selected 12 parameters, for which we defined between two to five potential values (Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors measured the fit between the empirical and simulated cover time series using an objective function.
source: We measured the fit between the empirical and simulated cover time series using an objective function.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The objective function measures the performance of a given run by calculating the Euclidian distance between the empirical and simulated cover time series, averaged over all the taxa.
source: The objective function measures the performance of a given run by calculating the Euclidian distance between the empirical and simulated cover time series (averaged over five replicates), averaged over all the taxa (Appendix 3: §3.2).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors generated a null distribution of performance values for each empirical dataset by randomizing cover values within each row and calculating the distance from the original datasets.
source: To compare the performance of model runs to a null expectation, we generated a null distribution of performance values for each empirical dataset by randomizing cover values within each row and calculating the distance from the original datasets.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the calibration methodology.

claim: The authors used a hierarchical approach to assess whether the different processes implemented in the model produce ecologically realistic patterns.
source: Following the recommendation of Kubicek et al. (2015), and aligned with the approach of pattern-oriented modeling (Grimm et al., 2005), we used a hierarchical approach to assess whether the different processes implemented in our model—starting from the those occurring at the lowest scales, to those affecting the entire system—produce ecologically realistic patterns by comparing them to expectations formulated a priori.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation methodology, with citations (Kubicek et al. (2015) and Grimm et al. (2005)).

claim: The authors based several of the expectations using the classification of life-history strategies of Grime (1977) into competitive, stress-tolerant and ruderal functional groups.
source: We based several of the expectations using the classification of life-history strategies of Grime (1977) into competitive, stress-tolerant and ruderal (CSR) (or weedy) functional groups—﻿a classification which was adapted to corals (Darling et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation methodology, with citations (Grime (1977) and Darling et al. (2012)).

claim: The authors expected colony lateral growth to equal the species growth rate in absence of spatial interaction and to decrease as space becomes saturated by colonies.
source: We assessed the following processes of our model: (i) we expected colony lateral growth to equal the species growth rate in absence of spatial interaction and to decrease as space becomes saturated by colonies
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation expectations.

claim: The authors expected recruitment rate to increase as a population grows from low initial cover, and then decrease as space saturates.
source: (ii) recruitment rate should increase as a population grows from low initial cover, and then decrease as space saturates
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation expectations.

claim: The authors expected the competitive species to dominate the community under low-disturbance regimes, and ruderal or stress-tolerant species otherwise.
source: for competition under different (iii) disturbance-regime intensities—we expected the competitive species to dominate the community under low-disturbance regimes, and ruderal or stress-tolerant species otherwise
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation expectations.

claim: The authors expected species with higher colony fecundity or brooding mode of larval development to dominate the community under low connectivity, and the competitive ones otherwise.
source: (iv) larval connectivity—we expected species with higher colony fecundity or brooding mode of larval development to dominate the community under low connectivity, and the competitive ones otherwise
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation expectations.

claim: The authors expected that under low grazing pressure, the benthic community should be dominated by algae, and by corals otherwise.
source: (v) grazing—under low grazing pressure, the benthic community should be dominated by algae, and by corals otherwise.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the validation expectations.

claim: The authors' goal for the global sensitivity analysis was to estimate the sensitivity of the predicted dynamics of the model to parameter variation during a process of recovery after a strong pulse disturbance.
source: Our goal was to estimate the sensitivity of the predicted dynamics of the model to parameter variation during a process of recovery after a strong pulse disturbance.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis objectives.

claim: The authors constructed a global sensitivity analysis for 10 of the calibrated parameters and six additional parameters with high uncertainty.
source: We constructed a global sensitivity analysis for 10 of the calibrated parameters and six additional parameters with high uncertainty (Appendix 6—table 1).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis design.

claim: The authors simulated the model for 10 years with a bleaching event of an intensity of 12 degree-heating weeks occurring after 4 years for the sensitivity analysis.
source: We simulated our model for 10 years with a bleaching event of an intensity of 12 degree-heating weeks occurring after 4 years.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis design.

claim: The authors assessed model sensitivity 6 years after the disturbance.
source: We consequently assessed model sensitivity 6 years after the disturbance, a time when the communities in most runs were still recovering.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis design.

claim: The authors defined five response variables for the sensitivity analysis: total coral cover, difference of total coral cover at year 10 and just after the bleaching event, Pielou's evenness, coral species richness, and number of recruits m⁻².
source: We defined five response variables that represent the ecological state of the community at the end of the simulation: (i) total coral cover, (ii) difference of total coral cover at year 10 and just after the bleaching event, (iii) Pielou's evenness, (iv) coral species richness (only the species with ≥1% cover), and (v) number of recruits m−2.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis design.

claim: The authors sampled 1000 combinations of parameter values from a continuous parameter space using Latin hypercube sampling and uniform-sampling distributions for each site.
source: For each site, we sampled 1000 combinations of parameter values from a continuous parameter space using Latin hypercube sampling and uniform-sampling distributions.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis methodology.

claim: The authors fitted boosted regression trees on the input parameter values for each response variable to estimate the relative importance of the parameters.
source: We then fitted boosted regression trees on the input parameter values for each response variable—the procedure provides the respective influence of each predictor (i.e. model parameter) on the variation of the response variable in question.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the sensitivity analysis methodology.

claim: Model performance varies between 28 and 10, with lower values indicating better performance.
source: Model performance (the Euclidian distance between the empirical and simulated cover time series averaged over all taxa) varies between 28 and 10 (lower values = better performance)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: All model performance values were lower than the lower 95% confidence bound of the random distribution.
source: and were all lower than the lower 95% confidence bound of the random distribution (Appendix 3—figure 9).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: The model outputs population dynamics closer to the empirical data compared to random.
source: This shows that, despite the model's complexity and parameter uncertainty, the model outputs population dynamics closer to the empirical data compared to random.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: The best performance values converged toward 10 among the three sites.
source: The best performance values converged toward 10 among the three sites (i.e. minimum ± standard error: 10.93 ± 3.677, 10.89 ± 2.872, 10.39 ± 3.119 for Fond Boucher, Pointe Borgnesse and Ilet à Rats, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: With the combination of parameter estimates yielding the best fit, the model produces time series of total coral cover similar to the empirical ones for each site.
source: With the combination of parameter estimates yielding the best fit, the model produces time series of total coral cover similar to the empirical ones for each site (Figure 3; Appendix 3—figure 14; Appendix 3—figure 15).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to figures.

claim: The difference between the simulated and real total coral cover does not exceed 15, 20, and 11% for Fond Boucher, Pointe Borgnesse and Ilet à Rats, respectively.
source: The difference between the simulated and real total coral cover does not exceed 15, 20, and 11% for Fond Boucher, Pointe Borgnesse and Ilet à Rats, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: The cover difference of individual coral populations never exceeds 8%.
source: Results at the species level are more variable, but the cover difference of individual coral populations never exceeds 8%.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: For some species, the simulated cover closely predicts the empirical data.
source: For some species, the simulated cover closely predicts the empirical data—for instance, O. faveolata and O. annularis at Ilet à Rats (Figure 3) and A. agaricites and S. siderea at Fond Boucher (Appendix 3—figure 14).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to figures.

claim: The model failed to predict the population dynamics of some species accurately.
source: The model failed to predict the population dynamics of some other species accurately
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: In the simulated reefs, M. mirabilis, M. decactis and P. furcata became the dominant species at Fond Boucher.
source: for instance, in the simulated reefs, M. mirabilis, M. decactis and P. furcata became the dominant species, while the cover of P. atreoides and M. meandrites approached zero at Fond Boucher
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: M. mirabilis outcompeted O. annularis, O. faveolata, O. franksi and P. astreoides at Pointe Borgnesse in the simulated reefs.
source: M. mirabilis outcompeted O. annularis, O. faveolata, O. franksi and P. astreoides at Pointe Borgnesse (Appendix 3—figure 14; Appendix 3—figure 15)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: The P. astreoides's population decreased at Ilet à Rats in the simulated reefs.
source: while the P. astreoides's population decreased at Ilet à Rats (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The simulated cover of algae closely mimics the empirical data for most algal groups.
source: The simulated cover of algae also closely mimics the empirical data for most algal groups (Figure 3; Appendix 3—figure 14; Appendix 3—figure 15).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to figures.

claim: The difference of percentage cover is the highest for turf and reaches a maximum of 29, 22% and 24% for Fond Boucher, Pointe Borgnesse and Ilet à Rats, respectively.
source: The difference of percentage cover is the highest for turf and reaches a maximum of 29, 22% and 24% for Fond Boucher, Pointe Borgnesse and Ilet à Rats, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: Turf cover generally fluctuates by >20%, a pattern that the model was able to reproduce at all three sites.
source: Turf cover generally fluctuates by >20%, a pattern that our model was able to reproduce at all three sites (Figure 3; Appendix 3—figure 14; Appendix 3—figure 15).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to figures.

claim: Crustose coralline algae are systematically less abundant in the simulated reefs compared to the observed data.
source: Notably, crustose coralline algae are systematically less abundant in the simulated reefs compared to the observed data, a phenomenon we attempted to correct in the calibration procedure (Appendix 3: §3.3).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration.

claim: The model could not reproduce the high cover of Halimeda spp. observed at Ilet à Rats compared to the other sites.
source: Finally, the model could not reproduce the high cover of Halimeda spp. observed at Ilet à Rats (Figure 3) compared to the other sites.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the model calibration, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The hierarchically structured validation shows that the model produces ecologically realistic population dynamics under different environmental conditions.
source: The hierarchically structured validation shows that the model produces ecologically realistic population dynamics under different environmental conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Coral colonies grew at their species-specific growth rate at low population density.
source: Coral colonies grew ipso facto at their species-specific growth rate at low population density.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: As space filled up, colonies began constraining each other spatially and their growth rates decreased until eventual stasis.
source: However, as space filled up, colonies began constraining each other spatially and their growth rates decreased until eventual stasis (Appendix 5—figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Weedy and stress-tolerant species produced bell-shape recruitment patterns.
source: Weedy (Agaricia tenuifolia) and stress-tolerant species (Echinophyllia orpheensis) produced bell-shape recruitment patterns (Appendix 5—figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Recruitment rate for competitive species was initially high and only decreased as cover occupancy increased.
source: In contrast, recruitment rate for competitive species (Acropora gemmifera) was initially high and only decreased as cover occupancy increased.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: In both the Western Atlantic and Eastern Pacific communities, the competitive species dominated the coral community under low wave exposure.
source: In both the Western Atlantic and Eastern Pacific communities (we compared the two functionally distinct coral communities in the rest of the analysis), the competitive species dominated the coral community under low wave exposure (Appendix 5—figure 10, 11, 14).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Higher wave exposure reduced the cover of competitive species because colonies were dislodged at a certain colony size.
source: Higher wave exposure reduced the cover of competitive species because colonies were dislodged at a certain colony size, which reduced recruitment rate and provided other species with more available space to grow and recruit.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: In the Western Atlantic community, increased availability of space favoured the weedy species over the stress-tolerant species.
source: In the Western Atlantic community, increased availability of space favoured the weedy species (Madracis pharencis) over the stress-tolerant species (Orbicella annularis), principally because of the former's brooding mode of larval development (twice a year), faster growth rate, and high wave-resistance of its growth form (digitate).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Species coexisted in the Eastern Pacific community under the highest-intensity disturbances.
source: In contrast, species coexisted in the Eastern Pacific community under the highest-intensity disturbances (Appendix 5—figure 14).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: Population(s) recovered to pre-disturbance cover after only one year, regardless of the intensity of the event.
source: Population(s) recovered to pre-disturbance cover after only one year, regardless of the intensity of the event.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the hierarchically structured validation.

claim: This recovery is faster than most dynamics observed in real reef systems and arises because the authors imposed a constant and high number of larvae coming from the regional pool.
